name: reduction-to-a-false-hypothesis
description: A reduction whose hypothesis is unsatisfiable on the object it names passes every sorry census and axiom probe, because it is a theorem; check satisfiability before crediting it, and before asking another team to adopt it.

`Pic0.universallyClosed_of_ambient` reduced properness of `Pic⁰` to `UniversallyClosed (PicScheme C).hom`. True, sorry-free, axiom-clean, recommended by its roadmap row as "worth trying first" for three sessions — and it reduces **nothing**: mathlib derives `QuasiCompact` from `UniversallyClosed` (the priority-900 instance, which is *why* `IsProper` has no quasi-compactness field), and `Spec k` is compact, so the hypothesis forces `CompactSpace (PicScheme C).left` while `Pic_{C/k}` is an infinite disjoint union over `deg ∈ ℤ` — the very clause `HasPicScheme` bundles.

**Why:** no standard check can see this. A sorry census sees no sorry; `#print axioms` reports clean; the build is green. A theorem with an unsatisfiable antecedent *is* a theorem. This is [[trap-c-on-a-negative-result]] pointing the other way: there, an in-tree `¬P` refuted nothing because its hypotheses could not hold; here a `P → Q` reduced nothing for the same reason.

**How to apply:** before crediting "X reduces to Y on object Z", ask whether Y can hold at Z — especially when Z is an *ambient* object and the sharp statement was about a subobject. Two specific tripwires: `UniversallyClosed`/`IsProper` over an affine base silently carry finiteness of the source (via `QuasiCompact`), so they are false on anything with infinitely many components; and a "second, independent route" that moves work onto a *bigger* object deserves the satisfiability check first, not last. The escalation matters: I had asked another team to add the false conjunct to a shared interface class before checking. Withdraw such asks the moment the check fails, and retract at the docstring, the roadmap row, and the graph node — see [[retract-where-the-claim-is]].

Three sessions named porting the sibling project's two-chart Čech machinery as the live route for AJC's tangent-space clause (iii). Measured: the port is 60 files / 17k lines, all sorry-free — a plausible multi-session job. It still cannot work. The sibling's `Scheme.CechPic` is a *self-contained definitional* Picard group whose only bridge to invertible sheaves, `cechPicEquivPic`, carries `[IsAffine X]` irremovably (it needs a trivializing basic open per point plus `Module.Invertible.span_tensor_free_eq_top` over `Γ(X,⊤)`). Clause (iii) lives on `C ×_k Spec k[ε]`, a proper curve — non-affine *precisely because* the interesting `ε`-kernel is nonzero. The one hypothesis the dictionary needs is what the problem structurally denies.

**Why:** the size question and the connectivity question are independent, and only the first is easy to measure. Paying 17k lines leaves you holding a class in `X.CechPic` with no theorem relating it to `LineBundle.OnProduct`. This is [[diff-api-by-face-not-name]] and [[matching-the-category-is-not-matching-the-object]] at the scale of a whole subsystem.

**How to apply:** before pricing a port, ask what *carrier* you end up holding and whether it has the face your consumer needs. The test is one grep for the comparison theorem between the two carriers, plus a read of its **binders** — an affineness or finiteness side condition on the comparison can void the whole port. When both the import closure and the declaration-reference count come out large (here 13.7k and 17k), treat that agreement as a signal to check connectivity rather than to start porting; per [[price-a-port-by-declaration-reference]] a genuine port usually collapses under declaration-reference pricing, and one that does not is suspicious.
